title: Checking Continuity of a Two-Piece Function at Its Join
author: Muhammad Abdullah Athar
problemStatement: Graph the function defined by f(x) = x + 1 for x < 1 and f(x) = 3 - x for x >= 1. Decide whether the two pieces join cleanly at x = 1 or leave a gap, and support the decision with one-sided limits.

steps.title: Take the left-hand limit
steps.explanation: Approaching 1 through values below it uses the first formula, whose limiting height is 2, although the point (1, 2) itself is not drawn from that branch.
steps.why: Only x < 1 lies in the domain of the first piece, so the left branch must be evaluated by a limit rather than by direct assignment.

steps.title: Take the right-hand limit and the function value
steps.explanation: The second piece both approaches 2 and equals 2 at x = 1, since the inequality there includes the endpoint.
steps.why: Continuity requires the value at the point to agree with the limit, which is why f(1) must be computed from the branch that owns x = 1.

steps.title: Compare and describe the picture
steps.explanation: All three quantities match, so the graph is an unbroken tent: a rising ray of slope 1 meeting a falling ray of slope -1 at the peak (1, 2), forming a corner rather than a gap.
steps.why: Equal one-sided limits give continuity, but unequal one-sided slopes mean the function is not differentiable at the join.

steps.title: Set a window that shows the join
steps.explanation: Plotting both pieces over this window centers the frame on x = 1 so the peak and both rays are visible with room to read the change of direction.
steps.why: Some packages draw each piece on its own interval, and a window that ends at x = 1 hides whether the pieces actually touch.
